Equal Chords in Crossing Circles

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Two circles cross and two lines pass through the crossing point; drag the points and watch the two coloured pieces.
How to play: Drag P, Q, A or D, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the names, the claim and the helper lines.

Drag P or Q to change the crossing and the circles; drag A or D to swing the two lines. Arrow keys move a focused point, Shift makes a bigger step.

AB = CD: the two lines through P make equal angles with PQ, so the pieces of them inside the circles are equal.

Adjust
Look for the math

Two circles cross at P and Q. A straight line through P leaves one circle at A and the other at B; another line, leaning the same way from PQ, leaves them at C and D. Surprisingly, the two chords AB and CD are the same length.

The old book's claim

The page quotes exercise 7 from Hall and Stevens's 1904 book: If two circles cut one another, any two straight lines drawn through a point of section, making equal angles with the common chord, and terminated by the circumferences, are equal. The logic test checked this on more than seven hundred layouts, with slanted, horizontal and vertical common chords: AB = CD to within one millionth of a drawing unit. Straight lines have no arrow, so an angle of 180° − θ counts as the same lean as θ. The claim is about proper chords: when a line only touches a circle at P, one end collapses onto P and there is no chord to measure. The status line says so instead of claiming equality.

How the applet draws the second line

Start with A on the first circle and B on the second, both on one line through P. Mirror A and B across the common chord PQ, and join each mirror to P. The second meeting of those lines with the same two circles is C and D, so the two lines are mirror images in PQ. That is exactly what the applet's AMoved and DMoved do, and it is why the two undirected angles with PQ match. Moving D instead of A runs the steps backwards. The logic test transcribed those steps straight from the bytecode and compared every constructed point over hundreds of configurations.

The line of centres

Draw through Q a line parallel to CD; it cuts chords C'D' that are equal to CD. The centres E and F lie on the perpendicular bisector of PQ, and C'D' is the reflection of AB in that line of centres. Hubert Shutrick's shorter proof says both chords are twice the projection of EF on them. Since EF is perpendicular to PQ while AB and CD lean equally from it, the projections match:

AB = CD = 2 · |projection of EF onto the chord|

The test checked this formula, the equality C'D' = CD and the symmetry in EF on every valid layout it generated; all passed.

Not the crossed-circles puzzle

Our sibling page Equal Angles in Crossed Circles asks a different question: a chord of one circle crosses the other at P and Q, and it proves ∠ASP = ∠BTQ from inscribed angles in two quadrilaterals. Here both lines go through the same crossing point P and the result is about equal lengths, not equal angles at different vertices. One harmless leftover stays from the Java code: its about-box still calls itself "Pythagorean Theorem, Proof #36". The panel's Adjust chord checkbox state is never copied into the canvas either, but the two radio buttons are mutually exclusive, so Adjust circles being on means chord mode is off, exactly as the applet behaves.

Tick the hint and then drag P. The dashed lines follow, C'D' stays level with CD, and the two numbers in the status line keep agreeing.
